questions.question: State the approximate composition of dry air and calculate the oxygen volume in 2.40 dm3 of air.
Describe the likely early atmosphere and explain why scientists use cautious language about it.
questions.modelAnswer: Volcanic gases; mainly CO2 and water vapour, small methane/ammonia, little/no O2. Formed billions of years ago, limited direct evidence; models inferred and revised.
markingPoints: Volcanic gases
mainly CO2 and water vapour, small methane/ammonia, little/no O2. Formed billions of years ago, limited direct evidence
models inferred and revised.

questions.question: Explain three processes that decreased atmospheric carbon dioxide over geological time.
questions.modelAnswer: Dissolved in oceans; photosynthesis removed CO2; carbonate shells/sediments formed limestone; carbon buried in fossil fuels/rocks. Explain storage/removal.
markingPoints: Dissolved in oceans
photosynthesis removed CO2
carbonate shells/sediments formed limestone
carbon buried in fossil fuels/rocks. Explain storage/removal.

questions.question: Explain how atmospheric oxygen increased and why it did not immediately accumulate when photosynthesis began.
questions.modelAnswer: Algae/plants photosynthesised, releasing O2; initially reacted with iron/rocks and other reducing materials/respiration; accumulated only after sinks became saturated/production exceeded removal.
markingPoints: Algae/plants photosynthesised, releasing O2
initially reacted with iron/rocks and other reducing materials/respiration
accumulated only after sinks became saturated/production exceeded removal.

questions.question: Explain the greenhouse effect as an energy-transfer sequence without saying greenhouse gases trap sunlight.
questions.modelAnswer: Short-wave solar radiation passes/absorbed by surface; Earth warms; emits long-wave IR; greenhouse gases absorb IR and re-emit in all directions; less net energy escapes, increasing surface temperature.
markingPoints: Short-wave solar radiation passes/absorbed by surface
Earth warms
emits long-wave IR
greenhouse gases absorb IR and re-emit in all directions
less net energy escapes, increasing surface temperature.

questions.question: Link human activities to increases in carbon dioxide and methane, giving at least two sources of each.
questions.modelAnswer: CO2: fossil-fuel combustion, deforestation, cement. CH4: cattle, rice, landfill, fossil-fuel extraction. Explain release/reduced uptake where relevant.
markingPoints: CO2: fossil-fuel combustion, deforestation, cement. CH4: cattle, rice, landfill, fossil-fuel extraction. Explain release/reduced uptake where relevant.

questions.question: Evaluate the claim that correlation between CO2 and global temperature proves CO2 causes warming.
questions.modelAnswer: Correlation alone not proof; confounders/feedback possible. But known IR mechanism, lab evidence, historical data, models and multiple independent observations support causation. Balanced evidence-based conclusion.
markingPoints: Correlation alone not proof
confounders/feedback possible. But known IR mechanism, lab evidence, historical data, models and multiple independent observations support causation. Balanced evidence-based conclusion.

questions.question: Explain why climate predictions have uncertainty but are still useful.
questions.modelAnswer: Future emissions unknown; complex feedback/cloud/ocean behaviour; model resolution/data limits; natural variation. Models tested against observations and give ranges/scenarios useful for risk decisions.
markingPoints: Future emissions unknown
complex feedback/cloud/ocean behaviour
model resolution/data limits
natural variation. Models tested against observations and give ranges/scenarios useful for risk decisions.

questions.question: Define carbon footprint and evaluate three ways a school could reduce it, including one limitation for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Total direct+indirect greenhouse gases as CO2e. Measures such as insulation/efficiency, renewable electricity, transport change, lower consumption/food waste; evaluate cost, intermittency, behaviour, embodied impacts, feasibility and data.
markingPoints: Total direct+indirect greenhouse gases as CO2e. Measures such as insulation/efficiency, renewable electricity, transport change, lower consumption/food waste
evaluate cost, intermittency, behaviour, embodied impacts, feasibility and data.

questions.question: For coal combustion, identify sources, formation and effects of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide and particulates.
questions.modelAnswer: S impurity burns -> SO2, acid rain/respiratory. High T N2+O2 -> NOx, acid rain/smog/respiratory. Limited O2 -> CO toxic. Soot/unburnt carbon -> particulates, lung damage/global dimming.
markingPoints: S impurity burns -> SO2, acid rain/respiratory. High T N2+O2 -> NOx, acid rain/smog/respiratory. Limited O2 -> CO toxic. Soot/unburnt carbon -> particulates, lung damage/global dimming.

questions.question: Distinguish a greenhouse gas from an atmospheric pollutant and explain why a substance may be both or mainly one.
questions.modelAnswer: Greenhouse classification concerns IR absorption/climate; pollutant concerns harmful concentration/effects. CO2 greenhouse gas, CO toxic pollutant not major greenhouse gas; effects depend on chemistry/lifetime/concentration.
markingPoints: Greenhouse classification concerns IR absorption/climate
pollutant concerns harmful concentration/effects. CO2 greenhouse gas, CO toxic pollutant not major greenhouse gas
effects depend on chemistry/lifetime/concentration.

questions.question: A policy reduces methane emissions quickly but CO2 only slowly. Explain why methane reduction can affect near-term warming while long-lived CO2 still matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Methane strong greenhouse gas but shorter atmospheric lifetime; cuts can reduce near-term forcing. CO2 accumulates/persists, so long-term warming depends on cumulative emissions.
markingPoints: Methane strong greenhouse gas but shorter atmospheric lifetime
cuts can reduce near-term forcing. CO2 accumulates/persists, so long-term warming depends on cumulative emissions.

questions.question: Explain how particulates can cause both health effects and global dimming.
questions.modelAnswer: Fine particles enter lungs/airways causing disease; scatter/absorb incoming sunlight so less reaches surface, producing cooling/dimming effect.
markingPoints: Fine particles enter lungs/airways causing disease
scatter/absorb incoming sunlight so less reaches surface, producing cooling/dimming effect.

questions.question: Compare carbon capture and storage with reforestation as carbon-footprint strategies.
questions.modelAnswer: CCS captures concentrated CO2, potential large scale but energy/cost/storage leakage/infrastructure. Trees remove CO2 and aid habitats but require land/time and carbon can be re-released by fire/felling. Contextual judgement.
markingPoints: CCS captures concentrated CO2, potential large scale but energy/cost/storage leakage/infrastructure. Trees remove CO2 and aid habitats but require land/time and carbon can be re-released by fire/felling. Contextual judgement.

questions.question: A graph shows temperature rising while solar output has no matching long-term rise. Explain how this evidence should be used in an argument.
questions.modelAnswer: Weakens solar-output explanation for trend; does not alone prove sole cause; combine with greenhouse mechanism, gas records and other forcings; distinguish correlation/evidence strength.
markingPoints: Weakens solar-output explanation for trend
does not alone prove sole cause
combine with greenhouse mechanism, gas records and other forcings
distinguish correlation/evidence strength.

questions.question: State the approximate percentages of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases in present-day dry air.
questions.modelAnswer: About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases including argon and approximately 0.04% carbon dioxide.
markingPoints: About 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and about 1% other gases including argon and approximately 0.04% carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Name the main gas believed to have formed Earth’s early atmosphere.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Why was there little or no oxygen in Earth’s early atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: There were no photosynthesising organisms initially, and any oxygen produced reacted with rocks/minerals.
markingPoints: There were no photosynthesising organisms initially, and any oxygen produced reacted with rocks/minerals.

questions.question: How did oceans help reduce the concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide?
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and became locked into carbonate sediments and rocks.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide dissolved in the oceans and became locked into carbonate sediments and rocks.

questions.question: How did photosynthetic algae and plants change Earth’s atmosphere?
questions.modelAnswer: They absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis, decreasing CO2 and increasing O2 over time.
markingPoints: They absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen by photosynthesis, decreasing CO2 and increasing O2 over time.

questions.question: Name three greenhouse gases.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.
markingPoints: Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour.

questions.question: Explain how greenhouse gases warm Earth’s surface.
questions.modelAnswer: Short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth; the surface emits infrared radiation; greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface.
markingPoints: Short-wave solar radiation reaches Earth
the surface emits infrared radiation
greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the surface.

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase atmospheric methane.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: cattle/rice farming, landfill and leaks during fossil-fuel extraction.
markingPoints: Examples: cattle/rice farming, landfill and leaks during fossil-fuel extraction.

questions.question: Give two human activities that increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
questions.modelAnswer: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation/land-use change.
markingPoints: Burning fossil fuels and deforestation/land-use change.

questions.question: State three possible consequences of global climate change.
questions.modelAnswer: Examples: sea-level rise, changing rainfall, more extreme weather, habitat loss, migration changes and reduced biodiversity/food security.
markingPoints: Examples: sea-level rise, changing rainfall, more extreme weather, habitat loss, migration changes and reduced biodiversity/food security.

questions.question: Why is peer review important when scientists publish climate research?
questions.modelAnswer: Other experts check the methods, evidence and reasoning, helping identify errors and improve confidence in conclusions.
markingPoints: Other experts check the methods, evidence and reasoning, helping identify errors and improve confidence in conclusions.

questions.question: What is a carbon footprint?
questions.modelAnswer: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
markingPoints: The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases emitted over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.

questions.question: How is sulfur dioxide formed when fossil fuels burn?
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen during combustion.
markingPoints: Sulfur impurities in the fuel react with oxygen during combustion.

questions.question: How are nitrogen oxides formed in a vehicle engine?
questions.modelAnswer: At high temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react.
markingPoints: At high temperatures, nitrogen and oxygen from the air react.

questions.question: State one environmental effect of sulfur dioxide and one of nitrogen oxides.
questions.modelAnswer: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain; nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and photochemical smog/respiratory problems.
markingPoints: Sulfur dioxide causes acid rain
nitrogen oxides cause acid rain and photochemical smog/respiratory problems.

questions.question: Explain how the early atmosphere changed as oceans and sedimentary carbonate rocks formed.
questions.modelAnswer: Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to oceans. CO₂ dissolved in oceans and was used by marine organisms; carbon became locked in shells/skeletons and carbonate sediments/rocks, reducing atmospheric CO₂.
markingPoints: Earth cooled and water vapour condensed to oceans. CO₂ dissolved in oceans and was used by marine organisms
carbon became locked in shells/skeletons and carbonate sediments/rocks, reducing atmospheric CO₂.

questions.question: Evaluate the statement: “A correlation between atmospheric CO₂ and global temperature proves CO₂ is the only cause.”
questions.modelAnswer: Correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors affect climate. However, greenhouse mechanism is established and multiple independent records/models support a CO₂ contribution. Data uncertainties and confounding variables should be considered; “only cause” is unjustified.
markingPoints: Correlation alone does not prove causation and other factors affect climate. However, greenhouse mechanism is established and multiple independent records/models support a CO₂ contribution. Data uncertainties and confounding variables should be considered
“only cause” is unjustified.

questions.question: Explain how sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides cause environmental harm and how their emissions can be reduced.
questions.modelAnswer: They form acidic solutions/acid rain, damaging ecosystems/buildings; NOx also contributes to respiratory problems/smog. Use low-sulfur fuels/flue-gas desulfurisation, catalytic converters, lower combustion temperatures and reduced fossil-fuel use.
markingPoints: They form acidic solutions/acid rain, damaging ecosystems/buildings
NOx also contributes to respiratory problems/smog. Use low-sulfur fuels/flue-gas desulfurisation, catalytic converters, lower combustion temperatures and reduced fossil-fuel use.

questions.question: Explain why carbon monoxide is produced in a faulty gas heater and why it is dangerous.
questions.modelAnswer: Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, forming CO. CO is colourless/odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing blood oxygen transport and potentially causing death.
markingPoints: Insufficient oxygen causes incomplete combustion, forming CO. CO is colourless/odourless and binds strongly to haemoglobin, reducing blood oxygen transport and potentially causing death.

questions.question: Explain how photosynthetic organisms altered atmospheric gases and enabled complex animal life.
questions.modelAnswer: Photosynthesis removed CO₂ and released O₂. Oxygen accumulated, enabling efficient aerobic respiration; it also enabled ozone formation, reducing harmful UV at Earth’s surface.
markingPoints: Photosynthesis removed CO₂ and released O₂. Oxygen accumulated, enabling efficient aerobic respiration
it also enabled ozone formation, reducing harmful UV at Earth’s surface.

questions.question: Explain how ice-core and sediment evidence can be used to reconstruct past atmospheric composition and climate.
questions.modelAnswer: Trapped air bubbles preserve samples of past atmosphere; isotope ratios and sediment/pollen records act as climate proxies; layers can be dated. Agreement between independent records increases confidence, but resolution and dating uncertainty limit conclusions.
markingPoints: Trapped air bubbles preserve samples of past atmosphere
isotope ratios and sediment/pollen records act as climate proxies
layers can be dated. Agreement between independent records increases confidence, but resolution and dating uncertainty limit conclusions.

questions.question: Evaluate the claim that a short period of cooler weather disproves global warming.
questions.modelAnswer: Weather is short-term and local; climate is a long-term global pattern. Natural variability can cause cool periods within a warming trend. Use long-term global datasets rather than one event.
markingPoints: Weather is short-term and local
climate is a long-term global pattern. Natural variability can cause cool periods within a warming trend. Use long-term global datasets rather than one event.

questions.question: Describe how to compare particulate pollution at two roadside locations using deposited particles.
questions.modelAnswer: Expose equal-area collection surfaces for the same time and height; use several samples at each site; keep weather period comparable; count particles or measure covered area with a microscope/image analysis; calculate means; record traffic and weather as possible confounders.
markingPoints: Expose equal-area collection surfaces for the same time and height
use several samples at each site
keep weather period comparable
count particles or measure covered area with a microscope/image analysis
calculate means
record traffic and weather as possible confounders.

questions.question: Explain why correlation between atmospheric carbon dioxide and global temperature is not, by itself, complete proof of causation.
questions.modelAnswer: Correlation can be influenced by other variables and feedbacks. Causal confidence comes from mechanism, controlled/physical evidence, modelling and multiple independent datasets, not correlation alone.
markingPoints: Correlation can be influenced by other variables and feedbacks. Causal confidence comes from mechanism, controlled/physical evidence, modelling and multiple independent datasets, not correlation alone.

questions.question: A pollution sensor is calibrated incorrectly and reads 5 ppm too high. Explain why taking more readings does not improve accuracy.
questions.modelAnswer: All readings have the same systematic positive bias. More readings may improve precision of the mean but it remains about 5 ppm too high; recalibration is needed.
markingPoints: All readings have the same systematic positive bias. More readings may improve precision of the mean but it remains about 5 ppm too high
recalibration is needed.

questions.question: Explain why climate models should be tested against historical data before being used for projections.
questions.modelAnswer: Historical data provide outcomes not used or partly used in development. If a model reproduces observed patterns within uncertainty, confidence increases; failures reveal assumptions or processes needing revision.
markingPoints: Historical data provide outcomes not used or partly used in development. If a model reproduces observed patterns within uncertainty, confidence increases
failures reveal assumptions or processes needing revision.
